editor_note: Ownership transparency and controls over distant operations dominate: states fight FinCEN's BOI rollback, a sanctions settlement punishes weak subsidiary oversight, and Canadian and French regulators land sizeable marketing and cookie penalties.

bottom_line.text: 21 AGs sue to restore BOI reporting; keep your own ownership verification in KYC and vendor diligence.
Extreme Networks pays $2.5M over Russian subsidiary; test subsidiary sanctions controls and self-disclosure readiness.
Rogers ordered to pay $15M for deceptive marketing; review plan and pricing claims in Canada.
CNIL fines Fnac Darty €7M over cookies; verify app and site consent before trackers fire.

cards.title: 21 attorneys general sue FinCEN to restore beneficial ownership reporting
cards.summary: A coalition of 21 attorneys general sued FinCEN in federal court in Oregon, challenging a rule that exempts U.S. companies from beneficial ownership reporting and commits the agency to deleting data already filed.
cards.impact: Keep collecting ownership data through your own KYC and third-party diligence; do not assume the federal BOI database will be available or stable.

cards.title: 'Near miss' on self-disclosure costs Extreme Networks $2.5M in sanctions case
cards.summary: Extreme Networks, a North Carolina networking company, will pay $2.5 million to settle charges that its Russian subsidiary repeatedly violated U.S. sanctions, a case highlighting the difficulty of overseeing foreign subsidiaries and qualifying for voluntary self-disclosure credit.
cards.impact: Test sanctions controls at foreign subsidiaries and make sure your escalation path can support a timely, complete voluntary self-disclosure.

cards.title: D.C. Circuit denies SEC award to whistleblower who first went to the media
cards.summary: The D.C. Circuit held that a whistleblower whose tip to a journalist led to successful SEC sanctions did not qualify for a Dodd-Frank whistleblower award, a precedent advocates call harmful to media-first whistleblowers.
cards.impact: Expect whistleblowers to be steered toward direct SEC reporting; keep internal channels credible so concerns surface to you first.

cards.title: Virginia mental health professional charged in $49M Medicaid fraud scheme
cards.summary: A federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia indicted a North Chesterfield mental health professional over an alleged $49 million fraud scheme involving mental health crisis services billed to Medicaid.
cards.impact: Healthcare providers should review billing audits for crisis and behavioral-health services, a recurring target of federal fraud enforcement.

cards.title: Former Army official pleads guilty to bribery and major fraud tied to Hawaii defense contracts
cards.summary: A former U.S. Army official pleaded guilty to conspiracy, bribery and major fraud charges connected to defense contracts in Hawaii.
cards.impact: Government contractors should recheck gifts, hospitality and conflict-of-interest controls around contracting officers and program staff.

cards.title: Labor Department recovers $603K in overtime for 829 workers at Indiana auto parts maker
cards.summary: The U.S. Department of Labor recovered $603,953 in back wages for 829 workers after finding an Indianapolis-area vehicle parts manufacturer failed to properly calculate overtime.
cards.impact: Audit regular-rate calculations, especially where bonuses or shift premiums apply; overtime miscalculation affects whole workforces at once.

cards.title: Justice Department releases eighth annual Elder Justice report
cards.summary: The DOJ Civil Division released its annual report to Congress summarizing enforcement, victim support and training efforts to combat elder fraud and abuse.
cards.impact: Financial institutions and care providers can use the report to benchmark elder-fraud monitoring and escalation controls.

cards.title: Competition Tribunal orders Rogers to pay $15M penalty over deceptive wireless marketing
cards.summary: The Competition Tribunal ruled for the Competition Bureau in its case against Rogers, ordering a $15 million penalty over the marketing of its Infinite wireless plans.
cards.impact: Review marketing claims about 'unlimited' or similar plan features; Canadian regulators are winning deceptive-marketing cases with significant penalties.

cards.title: Canada, EU, US and allies issue joint statement on North Korea sanctions
cards.summary: Canada joined Australia, the EU, the US, the UK, Japan, South Korea and others in a joint statement on Democratic People's Republic of Korea sanctions.
cards.impact: Recheck DPRK exposure in screening, including IT-worker hiring and shipping counterparties, as allies coordinate enforcement messaging.

cards.title: Competition Bureau says Air Canada-United arrangement would harm competition on Canada-U.S. routes
cards.summary: Canada's Competition Bureau concluded that a proposed Air Canada-United Airlines arrangement would harm competition on key Canada-U.S. routes.
cards.impact: Companies planning joint ventures or co-operation agreements in Canada should expect close Bureau scrutiny and build competition analysis in early.

cards.title: Four charged in cross-border tobacco smuggling operation using rail
cards.summary: A multi-year joint CBSA and RCMP investigation in Saskatchewan into a transnational, cross-provincial rail smuggling operation led to 36 charges against four individuals.
cards.impact: Logistics and rail shippers should confirm cargo verification and customs controls can detect contraband moving through legitimate supply chains.

cards.title: CNIL fines Fnac Darty companies €7 million over cookies on website and mobile app
cards.summary: On 22 October 2026, France's CNIL fined Fnac Darty Participations et Services and Fnac Direct a total of €7 million for breaching the rules on cookies and other trackers.
cards.impact: Check that mobile apps, not only websites, obtain valid consent before trackers fire; CNIL keeps imposing multimillion-euro cookie fines.

cards.title: Dutch privacy authority warns debt collectors on responsible use of AI
cards.summary: A Dutch Data Protection Authority sample of 29 collection agencies found growing use of algorithms and AI, speeding up work but creating risks of inaccurate decisions; the regulator is informing the sector on responsible use.
cards.impact: Firms using AI in collections or credit decisions should document accuracy checks and human review ahead of EU AI Act obligations.

cards.title: MEP says Amazon visit shows need for EU workplace rules on AI
cards.summary: MEP Li Andersson told Euractiv that algorithmic management poses a key challenge for workers and that a visit to Amazon showed the need for EU workplace rules on AI.
cards.impact: Inventory algorithmic management tools used on staff; an EU initiative could add transparency and consultation duties.

6f15e990bdf6.headline: 21 attorneys general sue FinCEN to restore beneficial ownership reporting
6f15e990bdf6.dek: States say FinCEN's rollback of Corporate Transparency Act reporting, and its plan to delete filed data, is unlawful.
6f15e990bdf6.body_md:
Twenty-one state and district attorneys general have gone to court to revive beneficial ownership reporting under the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA). The suit, filed on 27 October 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon, targets a Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) rule that removed the reporting duty for almost all businesses.

### The key facts

The coalition is led by Oregon and Illinois and includes California, Minnesota, New York, Massachusetts, Washington, the District of Columbia and others. According to the Minnesota attorney general, FinCEN issued the rule in August 2026, exempting what the states describe as 99.9% of businesses. Per the California attorney general, the rule exempts all U.S. companies and individuals, relieves foreign companies from reporting U.S. persons who are beneficial owners, and commits FinCEN to deleting ownership information already filed by domestic companies. FinCEN's stated view is that collecting the data does not serve the public interest.

The states argue the rule exceeds FinCEN's statutory authority and violates the CTA and the Administrative Procedure Act. They say FinCEN skipped required procedural steps, acted arbitrarily without a reasoned explanation, and failed to consult the Secretary of Homeland Security and the U.S. Attorney General as required before granting the exemption. They also contend that deleting the database would break several federal laws and could destroy evidence of unsolved crimes. The relief sought, per Minnesota, is to vacate the rule and require FinCEN to keep collecting and maintaining the database for law enforcement use.

### Background

Congress passed the CTA in 2021 with bipartisan support to create a Treasury database of who owns and controls companies, aimed at shell-company abuse in money laundering, bribery and fraud. States say they lose access to data they planned to use for tax and financial-protection enforcement. FinCEN's response to the suit was not reported in the sources reviewed, and the claims above are the states' allegations.

### What compliance teams should do

- Do not rely on the federal BOI registry for KYC or third-party onboarding; keep collecting and verifying ownership data yourself.
- If you previously filed BOI reports, keep internal copies and the supporting records, since the federal position may change again.
- Track the Oregon case and any state-level ownership disclosure laws that may fill the gap.
- Brief AML and procurement teams so beneficial-ownership checks stay in high-risk vendor and customer workflows.
